sections.html:
Muskogee is the seat of Muskogee County in eastern Oklahoma, about 50 miles southeast of Tulsa. The July 2025 population estimate is 36,760. It is a smaller city with an industrial past, a strict nuisance-abatement process and a tax question that surfaced in 2026 over court judgments, and those three things shape how sales go here. Owners can list, sell privately or take a cash offer, and the house's condition plus the city's code rules often decide which route makes sense.

The Arkansas, Verdigris and Grand rivers meet in the northeast corner of the city, an area once called Three Rivers. Elevation is low, around 600 feet, so check a flood map for any house on low ground or in a river valley before you set a price.

Muskogee Code Enforcement answers complaints about nuisance, zoning and property maintenance. The usual ones are high weeds and grass, trash and debris, vehicles parked on the grass, people living in an RV outside an RV park, inoperable vehicles and derelict structures. Complaints are anonymous, and because a legal process has to be followed the city asks residents to allow 15 to 20 business days for results. The number is (918) 684-6235.

If you own a vacant or neglected house, clear the yard before showings, since an open notice can turn up when a buyer searches city records. The city's ordinances treat vacant, abandoned or dilapidated structures as blight that lowers property values, and a house in that state may be a candidate for condemnation. Heirs and out-of-town owners should find out where their property stands early.

sections.h2: The $29.25 million judgment and your taxes
sections.html:
A city letter dated September 1, 2026 described three inverse condemnation cases against the city, filed in 2007, that ended in judgments totaling $29.25 million plus interest. They are England ($8.5 million), Taff ($6.5 million) and Lacey ($14.25 million), and each grew out of a property condemned and demolished under the nuisance abatement process about twenty years ago. The council approved settlement agreements on August 24, 2026.

Oklahoma cities pay court judgments from a sinking fund funded by property tax. If the whole amount went onto that fund, the city's estimate is roughly $450 a year per $100,000 of property valuation, based on figures from the Muskogee County Assessor. The decision would not be made until June 2027, any increase would start in October 2027, and it would stay on the tax rolls for three years. The council says it is looking at other ways to pay.

Treat this as a possibility rather than a set bill. A buyer comparing taxes may ask about it, and the letter is public on the city website.

sections.h2: How Muskogee County property taxes work
sections.html:
The county assessor sets fair cash value. The Oklahoma constitution requires real property to be assessed at no less than 11 percent and no more than 13.5 percent of that value, and the result is multiplied by the millage rate of the taxing districts. About 24 school districts operate in the county. Rates run from 76.22 mills in Wainwright to 105.49 in Hilldale, and a typical Muskogee address is taxed at 102.39 mills. Hilldale Public Schools covers a small southern part of Muskogee, so where a house sits can change the bill.

PaymentDue
First halfBy December 31
Second halfBy March 31

Because tax comes due in two halves, an early-year closing usually involves splitting the tax between you and the buyer or paying it off from your proceeds. The Muskogee County Treasurer is at 400 West Broadway, Room 220, (918) 682-0811. Call for the current balance on your parcel before you accept any offer.

Muskogee Public Schools covers most of the city limits. Hilldale Public Schools serves a small southern portion, and Fort Gibson Public Schools includes some areas in the east, so confirm the district for an address before you advertise a school. U.S. 62, 64 and 69, State Highways 16 and 165 and the Muskogee Turnpike serve the city, and commercial flights use Tulsa International, about 49 miles northwest.

Muskogee is warmer and more humid than much of Oklahoma, and it gets about 43 inches of rain a year, with May the wettest month. Heat, humidity and rain are hard on roofs, crawl spaces and older siding, so buyers often ask about moisture history. A recent roof or a documented drainage fix helps in a listing and in a cash conversation.

sections.h2: What Muskogee sellers usually run into
sections.html:
• Vacant or inherited houses with overgrown lots or open code notices
  • Older homes that need roof, foundation or plumbing work
  • Rentals that tenants left in poor condition
  • Owners worried about the possible tax increase
  • Sellers who live out of town and cannot manage repairs

A cash buyer will usually take a house as it is, including one with code issues, but the price reflects repairs and risk. Ask for the offer in writing and compare it with the net from a repaired and listed sale.

Before you talk price with anyone, collect the latest county tax statement, the name of your mortgage servicer, any code notice mailed to the property and receipts for roof, foundation or plumbing work. For an inherited house, add the paperwork that shows who has the authority to sell. If the tax question worries you, a buyer who sees that you know the situation and have the documents in order is usually easier to deal with, whether the sale is a listing or a cash purchase.

Start with a call about the address. Tell us the condition, who lives there, and whether a mortgage, lien or tax balance is attached. If an offer makes sense, you receive it in writing and can compare it with a listing without any deadline from us. After you accept, a title company researches ownership and liens, prepares the papers and sets a closing date. Mortgage payoff and tax balances come out of the proceeds at closing, and you keep the rest.

For a vacant or neglected house, ask the city about any open code notice first. A buyer who purchases as is may still want it resolved or disclosed, and knowing the status early avoids delays. Oklahoma sellers also need to deliver a disclosure or disclaimer statement before an offer is accepted.

faqs.q: How long does Muskogee code enforcement take to resolve a complaint?
faqs.a: The city asks residents to allow 15 to 20 business days because it has a legal process to follow. Complaints can be made by phone at (918) 684-6235 and stay anonymous.

faqs.q: Could Muskogee property taxes go up because of the court judgments?
faqs.a: Possibly. The city estimates about $450 a year per $100,000 of valuation if the full $29.25 million goes on the sinking fund. The decision would come in June 2027, and any increase would start in October 2027 and last three years.

faqs.q: What percent of value is real property assessed at in Oklahoma?
faqs.a: The state constitution sets the ratio between 11 and 13.5 percent of fair cash value. That result is multiplied by the millage rate.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Muskogee County?
faqs.a: At least half is due by December 31 and the second half by March 31. Call the county treasurer at (918) 682-0811 for a current balance.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Muskogee house that has a code violation?
faqs.a: Yes. Many buyers will purchase a house with open violations, but the notice may need to be resolved or disclosed at closing. Ask the city for the status and get any cash offer in writing.
